fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, part of it is just that I'm lazy about tooling in a very specific way. My time is the scarce resource, not the subscription cost. Every time you switch tools, you pay a tax: you relearn the prompting style, the quirks, what it's good at, what it quietly messes up. If I rotated between three or four of these things, I'd spend my energy benchmarking agents instead of doing research.

So I picked one that worked well enough and committed to it. With Claude Code, the thing I noticed early was that it was good at the parts of research code that actually eat my day. Not the clever algorithm, which I usually want to write myself anyway, but the plumbing: data loaders, evaluation scripts, config handling, refactoring a training loop so it runs on a different cluster. It reads the repo, figures out the conventions, and the output mostly fits in. And it lives in the terminal, which is where my students and I already are on the cluster. I don't have to drag a whole IDE environment onto a compute node.

The other reason is more subtle. When you stick with one tool for a long time, you build an intuition for when to trust it. I know which kinds of tasks I can hand off almost blindly and which ones I need to read line by line. That calibration is worth a lot, and it doesn't transfer across tools. A new agent might be five percent better on some benchmark, but I'd lose my sense of where it lies to me.

I'll admit there's some path dependence. My group converged on it, people share prompts and workflows, and it's easier to debug a student's setup when we're all using the same thing. If something clearly better came along, I'd switch. But "clearly better" has to beat the cost of relearning, and most of the time the differences I see are small compared to that.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a big part of it is just that switching has a real cost, and the gains from switching are usually smaller than people think.

With these tools, most of the value comes from knowing them really well. Over time you learn how to phrase a task, how much context to give, when to let it run on its own and when to step in, and what kinds of mistakes it tends to make. That intuition takes weeks to build. If I jump to a new tool every time someone on Twitter says it's two percent better on some benchmark, I reset all of that, and I end up spending more time evaluating tools than doing research.

It also fits how I actually work. A lot of research code runs on a cluster, in a terminal, over SSH, with messy experiment scripts and logs everywhere. Claude Code lives right there. It can read the files, run things, look at the output, and iterate, without me copying and pasting between windows. For the kind of work we do, like setting up experiments, writing evaluation scripts, digging through results, or refactoring some old codebase a student left behind, that workflow just feels natural.

And the models underneath have been strong and keep improving. When the tool I already use gets better every few months, the pressure to look elsewhere is pretty low.

That said, I don't think it's the only right answer. Some of my students use other tools and they're very productive with them. I do try other things occasionally, just to know where things stand. But my general philosophy is to pick something good, go deep, and only switch if there's a clear, large difference, not a marginal one. The field moves so fast that if you chase everything, you never get good at anything.

r001.rationale: The response clearly explains that sticking with Claude Code builds familiarity and intuition, while switching among competing tools spreads learning effort and resets that accumulated knowledge.

Honestly, a big part of it is just that my time budget for tool exploration is very limited. As faculty, the bottleneck in my research is almost never "which coding assistant is two percent better this month" — it's thinking time, student time, compute. So once a tool crosses the bar of being genuinely reliable, the returns on switching around are pretty small, and the cost of context-switching is real. Every tool has its own quirks, its own failure modes, and it takes a while before you develop good intuition for when to trust it and when to double-check.

With Claude Code, I've built up that intuition. I know what kinds of tasks I can hand off almost completely — refactoring experiment scripts, writing data processing pipelines, debugging a training run — and where I need to stay in the loop. That calibration is actually the valuable thing, more than any single feature. If I rotated between three tools, I'd be perpetually recalibrating.

I also like that it lives in the terminal and works directly with my actual repositories on the cluster. A lot of my work is long-running experiments on shared filesystems, and having an agent that can read logs, inspect outputs, and edit code in place fits that workflow much better than a chat window I'd have to copy-paste into.

That said, I do tell my students to try different tools — their workflows are still forming, and what's optimal for me isn't automatically optimal for them.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, part of it is just inertia, and I think I should own that rather than dress it up as a principled decision.

But there is a real reason underneath it. The value I get out of one of these tools isn't mostly in the tool — it's in the stuff I've accumulated around it. I know what it's good at, I know the specific ways it fails me, I've got a mental model of how to phrase things so it does what I want on the first try instead of the third. I have little setups in my repos, conventions I follow. None of that transfers when I switch. So when I try a competitor and it's ten percent better on some benchmark, that ten percent doesn't show up in my actual day, because I've thrown away the part that was doing the work.

There's also a time budget thing. Evaluating these tools properly is expensive. You can't tell from an afternoon — you need to run a real project through it, something with enough mess in it to expose the failure modes. That's a week, realistically. And the field moves fast enough that by the time you've done your careful comparison, everything's shifted and your conclusion is stale. So you'd be re-running that evaluation every couple months forever. I'd rather spend that week on research.

And I think people underrate how much the frontier models are converging on this. The gap between the top few is much smaller than the gap between someone who's learned to drive one of them well and someone who hasn't. So the return on switching is small and the return on getting better at the one you have is large. That's not a claim that Claude Code is the best — I genuinely don't know that, I haven't done the experiment. It's a claim that the experiment isn't worth running for me.

I'd say the one thing that would change my mind is a discontinuity. If something comes out that's doing a qualitatively different thing, not just scoring higher — then I'll look. I'm trying to be alert to that. But I don't want to confuse being alert to it with constantly shopping around.
